newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela bolivar slide not a concern - cenbank pres.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela bolivar slide not a concern - cenbank pres.

text.p: The recent slide of the Venezuelan bolivar, which has depreciated more than 0.5 percent in the last three days, is no cause for alarm, the central bank president said Thursday.
"We feel comfortable. We are within what was thought could be the normal movement of the bolivar this year," Antonio Casas Gonzalez told reporters after attending a human rights forum.
The bolivar currency closed weaker at 492.00/493.00 bolivars per dollar Wednesday compared with 490.00/490.75 per dollar at Tuesday's close.
But Casas said the exchange rate was still within the bands set by the central bank after liberalizing exchange markets 15 months ago.
At the start of 1997, the bank set a central parity of 472 bolivars per dollar, with maximum and minimum limits at 7.5 percent either side.
The central parity was set to depreciate at a monthly rate of 1.32 percent, in line with the government's 1997 inflation target of 30 to 35 percent.

The exchange rate has remained broadly stable for most of the year, depreciating just 2.5 percent to July 11, prompting economists and exporters to say that the local currency was increasingly overvalued.
Casas said the recent slide of the bolivar had been provoked by high levels of excess liquidity on money markets and a consequent drop in interest rates.
Yields on six-month central bank TEM bills, the benchmark from which wider interest rates are set, have fallen four percentage points in the past month.
To combat the high liquidity, the bank has stepped up the size of its weekly TEM auctions and increased the reserve requirement for commercial banks to 15 percent from 12 percent.
Casas said those two measures combined had soaked up about 500 billion bolivars ($1.01 billion) in the last 10 days.
"We have to continue monitoring because the indications are that excess liquidity is still high," Casas said.
